q: In ABC analysis, 'A' category items are characterized by:

options.A: Low consumption value but large in number
options.B: High annual consumption value but few in number
options.C: Medium value and medium in number
options.D: High unit price irrespective of consumption

q: The typical value distribution in ABC analysis is:
VED analysis classifies items as:
VED analysis is most useful for controlling:
FSN analysis classifies inventory on the basis of:
In FSN analysis, the letter 'N' denotes:

options.D: Non-moving items with no recent issues

q: A stock item in railway stores is:

options.A: An item held in the depot against anticipated future demand
options.B: An item procured only against a specific indent
options.C: An item issued directly to a work without storage
options.D: An item purchased on rate contract basis

q: A non-stock item is best described as:

options.A: An item always kept at the maximum level
options.B: An item issued only through bin cards
options.C: An item procured only against a specific demand or work
options.D: An item exempt from stock verification

q: The Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) is given by the formula:

options.A: Square root of (2 x ordering cost / demand)
options.B: Square root of (2 x annual demand x ordering cost / carrying cost per unit)
options.C: Annual demand divided by number of orders
options.D: Ordering cost plus carrying cost divided by two

q: At the economic order quantity, which of the following holds true?

options.A: Ordering cost is double the carrying cost
options.B: Total cost is at its maximum
options.C: Purchase price is at its minimum

q: Ordering cost is best defined as:

options.A: The cost incurred per purchase order, independent of order size
options.B: The cost of storing material per unit per year
options.C: The cost of capital blocked in inventory
options.D: The cost of obsolete stock written off

q: Which of the following is a component of inventory carrying cost?

options.C: Interest on capital blocked, storage, insurance and obsolescence

q: The re-order level is calculated as:

options.B: Average daily consumption x lead time plus safety stock
options.C: EOQ divided by number of orders per year
options.D: Safety stock minus lead time demand

q: Lead time in stores procurement comprises:

options.B: Only the transit time of goods
options.C: Only the inspection time after receipt
options.D: Administrative lead time plus procurement and supply lead time

q: The primary purpose of safety stock is to:

options.A: Absorb variations in demand and lead time during replenishment
options.C: Reduce the number of purchase orders

q: Fixing a maximum stock level mainly helps to:

options.C: Prevent overstocking and blocking of capital

q: The minimum stock level is equal to:

options.B: Re-order level minus normal consumption during normal lead time
options.C: Safety stock plus maximum lead time demand

q: The danger level of stock indicates that:

options.A: Stock has reached its maximum limit
options.C: The item should be declared surplus
options.D: Stock is below the minimum and emergency action is needed

q: Inventory turnover ratio is calculated as:

options.A: Annual issues divided by average inventory
options.B: Average inventory divided by annual receipts
options.C: Safety stock divided by re-order level

q: A high inventory turnover ratio generally indicates:

options.C: Efficient inventory use with low overstocking

q: A bin card maintained in the stores depot records:

options.A: Only the value of receipts and issues
options.B: Quantity received, issued and balance at the storage location
options.D: The sanction for write-off of shortages

q: How does the priced stores ledger differ from a bin card?

options.B: It is maintained by the Accounts department only
options.D: It maintains both quantity and value of each transaction

q: Perpetual inventory means:

options.A: Continuous recording of receipts and issues after every transaction
options.B: Stock verification once in five years
options.D: Ordering the full year's demand at once

q: Stock verification in railways is carried out by:

options.A: The depot storekeeper who holds the custody
options.C: Independent stock verifiers, not the custodian of the stores

q: The main object of stock verification is to:

options.B: Confirm that physical balances agree with the ledger balances

q: Surprise stock verification serves mainly as:

options.A: A method of fixing re-order levels
options.B: A substitute for the priced ledger
options.C: A means of valuing dead stock
options.D: A deterrent against pilferage and fraud

q: An excess of stores found during physical verification is:

options.A: Taken on charge in the stock books
options.B: Ignored if the value is small

q: A shortage of stores found during verification is:

options.B: Added to the bin card silently
options.C: Investigated and written off only with competent sanction

q: Surplus stock refers to:

options.A: Stock kept at the danger level
options.B: Stock in excess of reasonable anticipated requirements
options.D: Stock held only for emergency use

q: Dead stock consists of items:

options.D: With no movement or demand over a long period

q: The correct action on non-moving items identified by FSN analysis is to:

options.A: Declare them surplus and dispose of them by transfer, sale or auction
options.D: Shift them to the imprest stock

q: In stores terminology, a provision is:

options.A: The safety stock of vital spares
options.C: An estimate of requirements for a forthcoming period

q: The purpose of a periodic provision review is to:

options.B: Cancel or reduce indents that are no longer needed

q: Months' cover of a stock item is calculated as:

options.B: Safety stock multiplied by lead time
options.C: Re-order level divided by danger level
options.D: Stock on hand divided by average monthly consumption

q: A very low months' cover for a stock item signals that:

options.A: A stock-out is impending and supply must be expedited
options.B: The item should be declared surplus
options.C: The carrying cost is too high
options.D: The item can be made non-stock

q: ABC classification of items is based on:

options.C: Annual consumption value of each item

q: Control exercised over 'A' class items should be:

options.B: Tight, with frequent review and low safety stock

q: Control over 'C' class items is generally:

options.D: Loose, with larger lots and infrequent review

q: The EOQ model assumes that:

options.A: Demand rate and lead time remain constant
options.C: Ordering cost varies with order size

q: In the two-bin system of stock control:

options.A: Both bins are emptied before ordering
options.C: When the first bin empties, an order is placed and the second bin covers lead time demand

q: Stock-out cost refers to:

options.A: The cost of storing excess material
options.B: The loss from stoppage or delay due to non-availability of material
options.C: The cost of placing a purchase order

q: Total inventory cost is the sum of:

options.A: Ordering cost and inspection cost only
options.B: Carrying cost and stock-out cost only
options.D: Ordering cost, carrying cost and material cost

q: HML analysis classifies items on the basis of:

options.A: Unit price into High, Medium and Low
options.D: Lead time into long and short

q: XYZ analysis classifies inventory on the basis of:

options.C: Value of inventory held in stock

q: Imprest stock is:

options.B: A fixed small quantity held at sub-depots for immediate issue, replenished periodically
options.D: Stock held only for VIP works

q: Demand during lead time equals:

options.D: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days

q: Reaching the re-order point should trigger:

options.A: Initiation of purchase action for replenishment
options.B: Declaration of the item as surplus

q: ABC classification needs periodic reclassification because:

options.B: Unit prices are fixed by contract
options.C: Consumption patterns and prices change over time

q: For 'Vital' spares under VED analysis, the stocking policy is to:

options.A: Never stock them and buy on emergency
options.B: Always keep them in stock despite low consumption
options.D: Order them only once a year

q: Non-stock items involve which carrying cost?

options.A: Full carrying cost like stock items
options.D: No carrying cost, since they are not held in inventory

q: The stock verification report is submitted to:

options.A: The competent authority for orders on the discrepancies
options.D: No one; it is filed by the verifier

q: In railway stores practice, physical verification of depots is done:

options.C: At least once a year for every depot

q: The stock adjustment account is used to:

options.B: Record verification surpluses and shortages pending final orders

q: Which component of lead time is usually the longest?

options.D: Tendering and finalization of the purchase order

q: Safety stock needs to be higher when:

options.A: Variability of demand or lead time is high
options.D: The item is a 'C' class item

q: The maximum stock level is computed as:

options.C: Re-order level plus EOQ minus (minimum consumption x minimum lead time)
options.D: Minimum level plus maximum lead time demand

q: An abnormally low inventory turnover ratio indicates:

options.B: Overstocking or accumulation of dead stock

q: A rate contract for repeat items mainly reduces:

options.A: The unit price of all items
options.D: Ordering and administrative lead time for repeat purchases

q: When ABC and VED analyses are combined, which items get the tightest control?

options.A: A-V items: high consumption value and vital in nature
options.B: C-D items: low value and desirable
options.C: B-E items: medium value and essential
options.D: C-V items: low value but vital

q: Before surplus stores are disposed of by sale, they are first:

options.C: Offered for transfer to other railways or units that need them

q: Obsolescence of stored material is a part of:
The economic order quantity increases when:

options.D: Ordering cost rises relative to carrying cost

q: Perpetual inventory records help management to:

options.A: Detect discrepancies early without waiting for the annual count

q: Spare parts differ from general consumable stores in that they are:

options.C: Kept against equipment breakdown and maintenance needs

q: Provision for stock items is mainly based on:

options.B: Past consumption and anticipated future demand

q: Dead surplus stores are ultimately disposed of by:

options.D: Sale by auction after transfer options are exhausted

q: Re-order levels should be revised when:

options.A: Consumption pattern or lead time changes significantly

For control purposes, high-value 'A' items are verified:
The ultimate aim of inventory control is to ensure:

options.B: Zero purchase orders in a year
